messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Khải Nguyễn is a 31-year-old Vietnamese American carpenter, married, who presented for an initial assessment following a traumatic encounter with law enforcement approximately fourteen months ago. He was pulled over late one evening while driving home from a job site, tools still in the bed of his truck. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated rapidly: officers drew weapons, ordered him to the ground, and held him face-down on the asphalt for nearly twenty minutes while shouting commands he struggled to process through the fear. He was never charged with anything. He was told to leave. He drove home shaking, and in the weeks that followed, something in the way he moved through the world quietly broke apart.

In the months after the incident, Khải found that the ordinary texture of his days had become threaded with danger he could not reason away. At work, framing houses and fitting cabinetry in open sites and unfamiliar buildings, he grew acutely uncomfortable whenever he could not position himself with his back against a solid surface and a clear sightline to the room. On job sites where the layout forced him to work facing a wall, he would pause, reorient, sometimes fabricate a reason to move. His foreman noticed. Khải said nothing. The hypervigilance had a logic to it that felt unassailable to him — that night, he had been caught entirely exposed, face down, unable to see anything coming. He had come to believe that visibility was the only reliable margin of safety he had left.

The waiting was equally unbearable. When a lumber delivery ran late, when a colleague didn't text back within a reasonable window, when his wife was slow to answer her phone, Khải's body moved immediately into a state of braced anticipation — certain that the delay meant something bad was already in motion. He could not relax even in his own home, even when nothing was wrong, even when he told himself nothing was wrong. The knowledge of safety and the felt sense of safety had become entirely decoupled.

It was out of this unrelenting state of threat — the vigilance that never discharged, the waiting that never resolved — that Khải's coping began to take on a shape that worried him. He had started using drugs, marijuana initially, then occasionally something stronger, to blunt the edge of an alertness that left him exhausted by midday. The substances offered a temporary flattening of the threat signal, a few hours in which his back against a wall did not feel like a survival strategy. But the relief was short-lived, and in the spaces between, the hypervigilance returned sharper for having been suppressed. He also found himself caught in long loops of self-blame — replaying the stop, cataloguing every moment where he might have said something differently, moved differently, been less frightening to them, as though the violence of the encounter were a problem he had authored. He avoided thinking about the event directly, yet the rumination arrived sideways, in idle moments at the workbench or lying awake beside his wife. The self-blame and the effortful suppression did nothing to settle his nervous system; if anything, the unresolved cycling kept his body primed, the threat perception fed and never quieted.

The loop had become self-sealing. The constant sense of danger drove him toward the rumination, the avoidance, and the drug use as the only available relief valves — and those strategies, in turn, kept the threat alive, preventing any new information from reaching him that the world might, sometimes, be safe. His wife had begun asking questions he didn't know how to answer. He had turned down two larger contracts because the job sites felt unmanageable. It was this — the narrowing of his work, the growing distance from his wife, the recognition that he was losing ground — that finally brought him in. What Khải feared most was that something permanent had been done to him. What he hoped, more quietly, was that it hadn't.
